**The load-bearing half of the same sentence is true** — no payment names `F192`, `F193`, `F194`, `F195`, `F21`, or `F172` — under both derivations, verified by the authority driving `derivePayerMap` rather than reading the report.
**Nothing consumes the figure.** It appears once, in one `Assumption`, and no `Goal`, `Constraint`, acceptance criterion, or recorded command reads it. The spec skill states the contract: *"`Assumptions` remain presence with weak provenance and never block a gate."* `D30` keeps scalars out of hard `Constraints` precisely so binding text cannot depend on them.
**The maintainer ruled it recorded, not superseded.** The authority put both routes with the trade-off named — `D27`'s text says an approved artifact *found defective* is repaired by supersede, without qualification, so declining to supersede reads its purpose over its wording. The cost is accepted and permanent: this spec archives with a false measured figure, and archives are immutable. This entry is the only correction that will ever attach to it.
Owner: none. It is recorded so a future reader who cites that sentence finds the measurement that disproves it.

Finding.Title: ### F202 — `supersedeChainDepth`, the metric `D23` makes pilot's decider, records no cause and cannot see the cases that most inform pilot. **[verified]**
Finding.Body:
Measured **2026-09-08** at `5f5f95d`, from the supersede performed on this branch.
`D23` rules that *pilot is decided on `supersedeChainDepth`, not on the amendment count*. That figure is `chainDepth(changeId, buildPredecessorMap(projectRoot))` (`src/gates/ledger.ts:1165`) — a count of `<Replacement>` links and nothing else.
**The supersede verb records no reason.** After superseding `C-RECORD-TEST-ISOLATION`, its archived `run-ledger.xml` holds **two** `Decision` elements, both `gate="approve"`; the supersede itself wrote `status="superseded"`, the `<Replacement>` pointer, and the directory move. No cause, no class, no severity.
**Two consequences, both measured on this branch in one day.**
1. **Different classes increment identically.** The supersede here repaired an ownership contradiction that governs what an executor does — the close boundary. A supersede for a wrong figure nothing consumes would add the same 1. The number cannot tell a governing defect from a cosmetic one, which is the distinction a bounded-amendment regime would have to draw. 2. **The most informative case increments nothing.** [F201](#f201) is a defect found in an approved artifact and deliberately **not** superseded. `supersedeChainDepth` stays 1; nothing anywhere records that the event happened. So the metric systematically omits exactly the population that would justify a lighter route, and pilot is decided on a sample biased against its own question.
**A candidate discriminator, offered and not decided:** whether the defective text is **consumed** — is it inside a gate-binding element (`Goal`, `Constraint`, acceptance criterion, recorded `Command`, `Satisfies`) or referenced by one. That is mechanizable; the close-bound predicate already computes a similar property. The counter-argument belongs with it: a rule that lets an author reclassify text as non-governing invites the reclassification, and any amendment must still re-ratify with its own phrase and fingerprint, which is `RM-PILOT-APPROVAL`'s first constraint.
Owner: the maintainer, against `RM-PILOT-APPROVAL`. The cheap first step is not the regime but the instrument: record the cause on the supersede event, and record the declined-supersede outcome at all, so the number pilot rests on can answer the question pilot asks.

Finding.Title: ### F203 — a flush projection measured over buffer spans over-counts by one for every extra blank line, and the written base must come from `newlineCount`, not from the projection. **[verified]**
Finding.Body:
Measured **2026-09-08** at `99b5266`, during `C-RECORD-TEST-ISOLATION-2`'s record-writing task, raised by the executor and reproduced by the authority.
The approved plan projected the flush at **+129** lines using the rule *anchor-to-anchor span minus the trailing blank*. The buffer carried **two** blank lines before the `f196` anchor — an authority append — so that rule charged the extra blank to the **preceding** entry, `f192`, projecting a 35-line element where **34** landed. True growth was **128**, and the first write recorded `base="7730"` where the shipped `newlineCount` (`scripts/validate-record-retirement.ts:119-121`) reads **7729**.
**Caught in-window, not at review.** The executor compared the written base against `newlineCount`, found the mismatch, corrected the root to `base="7729" headroom="117"` with the ceiling untouched, and recorded a second attempt on the task. Nothing wrong reached the record; the base is now byte-verified against the file.
**The rule that follows.** Never derive a written base from a projection. Project only to check the ceiling is not breached, then **write the file and read `newlineCount` back** for the root attributes. When a projection is needed, cut at the next anchor dropping **all** trailing blanks, and count the landed element — open tag, `Title`, `<Body>`, prose, close — never the buffer span, which contains separators that belong to no entry.
**Same family as [F191](docs/plans/active/RM-GOVERNED-PATH/findings.xml)**: a measurement rule that attributes text to the wrong entry because nobody asked what the rule counts. There the strays were charter rows; here they are blank lines. **Ask what the rule attributes, not just whether it runs.**
The buffer's doubled separator has been normalised, so the artifact that caused this no longer exists — which is precisely why the rule is recorded here rather than left to be rediscovered.
